scope: Diff-based PR-gate security review for release 0.4.6 candidate 1 (the release-candidates governance system, ADRs 0005-0009) on the live feature branch, at head 90146c64bc85a882d8a425732907940d14f6b63a. ANCESTRY VERIFIED BEFORE CHOOSING THE RANGE: the branch was cut from main's squash fe04319a, whose tree I confirmed byte-identical to the integration tip 567a34f6 (both resolve to tree da58b3ac7e19cef4e40f53ebc55deb547a0c0cab), and the head is an ancestry-only reconciliation merge whose tree I confirmed byte-identical to its first parent 384dc391 (both bb0d5e39371addcd575d718ce1cdbdb9e2733d7e), proving the merge contributed zero content. The REAL content range reviewed is therefore fe04319a..384dc391: 10 commits, 79 files, +1491/-1234 (net +257 LOC), distributed as production code 11 files +331/-233, public assets 32 files +658/-675, tests 9 files +270/-168, specs 24 files +207/-156, plus the packaging manifest, the changelog and one context document. Zero dependency changes (the lock file is untouched; the manifest changes only its version line) and zero IaC surface (the repo carries no container, compose, Terraform or Pulumi definition at all). Subject matter: the canonical release-state filename decider and its read-side rewiring, the NEW candidate-archive verb behind a new CLI subcommand, canon entries for archived-candidate folders and the one-live-release refusal, a new doctor rule with a file-renaming auto-fix, deletion of the scaffolded segment lane, four pure archived-document renames, the 0.4.6 release definition, five appended architecture decisions, memory and projection refreshes, law and skill rewrites, and the version mint. Method, in priority order: verify the ancestry claims independently; review by hand every code path in the range that MOVES, RENAMES, WRITES or DELETES a file, for path traversal and symlink following; scan every added line for secrets, PII and private names; run the denylist push gate on the real range in both plausible stdin shapes; verify public-asset privacy with the tool and again with an independent grep; confirm the dependency delta; verify the version mint against the live package index; and audit test integrity, specifically that each deleted test is paired with a real feature deletion rather than silencing live behaviour. The full suite was not re-run (preflight is reported green at the content head: 2881 tests, mypy strict, import-linter 7/7); the three new test modules were executed directly. No exploit code, penetration tool or network scanner was run; the only network call was a read-only query of the public package index metadata.
verdict_reason:
APPROVED at 90146c64. None of the mandatory REQUEST_CHANGES triggers fires: no secret or credential appears in the range, the push gate exits 0, public-asset privacy reports ok, no test is disabled to hide a live failure, and no untrusted input reaches a privileged sink. One LOW documentation-honesty finding and five INFO items are recorded; none blocks.

I VERIFIED THE ANCESTRY BEFORE ACCEPTING THE REVIEW RANGE, because being handed the wrong range is the quiet way a review misses everything. Both claims hold independently: the branch's cut point and the integration tip resolve to the SAME tree object, and the head merge and its first parent resolve to the SAME tree object -- so the head is genuinely an ancestry-only reconciliation that contributed no content, and fe04319a..384dc391 is the complete content surface. Reviewing the head against the integration branch instead would have shown the same content plus reconciliation noise; reviewing the real range is both correct and tighter.

THE HEART OF THIS REVIEW IS THE NEW CODE THAT MOVES FILES, AND IT IS CONFINED BY CONSTRUCTION RATHER THAN BY VALIDATION. A new verb that renames a trio of documents into a computed directory is exactly where a path-traversal or symlink-following defect would live, so I traced every path component to its origin instead of reading the happy path. In the archive verb the destination is assembled as `specs_dir / 'releases' / release_id / f'rc-{rc}' / name`, and each component is unforgeable: `release_id` is not user input but a directory-entry NAME produced by iterating the releases directory, and an iteration entry is always a single path component -- it can never contain a separator and is never '.' or '..'; `rc` is an INTEGER, computed as one plus the maximum of integers parsed out of existing folder names by an anchored `^rc-(\d+)$` pattern, so interpolating it cannot introduce a separator; and the three trio filenames are module-level constants. There is no string concatenation of caller-supplied text anywhere in the path. Traversal is therefore not merely rejected, it is structurally impossible -- the strongest form of this property, and materially better than a validation check that could be bypassed or drift. The same reasoning clears the new doctor auto-fix: it renames using a name-replacement operation that substitutes only the FINAL path component and preserves the parent directory, so the rename cannot be aimed outside the source file's own directory no matter what path the issue carries; and the issue's path is itself produced by the doctor's own resolution through the same directory-entry-name derivation. Two further safety properties are present and deliberate rather than accidental: the archive directory is created with a bare make-directory call, with neither parent creation nor exist-tolerance, so it refuses loudly instead of clobbering or creating a path anywhere else; and the rename primitive used for the move does not follow a symlink at the SOURCE -- it relocates the link itself -- so even a planted symlink in the trio would be moved rather than written through to an external target.

THE VALIDATION GATE IN FRONT OF THE MOVE IS REAL AND TESTED. The verb refuses unless exactly one live release exists, the trio is present, the task document carries no open or reserved marker, and the phase is the closure phase; the multiple-live-release case is reported as an explicit error rather than guessed at. This matters because the move is destructive to layout: the refusals are what stop it running against a half-finished or ambiguous tree. Coverage is not asserted, it is present -- four of the seven new tests for this module exercise refusal paths (open tasks, reserved tasks, wrong phase, no live release) and three exercise the happy paths including the legacy-filename rename. I executed the three new modules directly: 15 tests, all pass.

SECRETS, PII AND PRIVATE NAMES OVER ADDED LINES -- CLEAN, ON EVERY SUBSET. Scanning only the added lines of the real content range returns ZERO hits for operator-home path prefixes, credential keywords, PEM private-key headers, private-IP and RFC1918 literals, personal e-mail domains, cloud access-key identifiers, platform token shapes, the operator's name, and every sibling repo slug on the denylist. A separate scan for assignment-shaped credentials (a credential keyword followed by a quoted six-or-more-character literal) also returns zero. Nothing required redaction because nothing matched.

DENYLIST PUSH GATE, RUN ON THE REAL RANGE, IN BOTH PLAUSIBLE SHAPES -- EXIT 0 EACH TIME. I fed the gate the actual pre-push stdin format via the absolute virtual-environment binary, once as a new-branch push (zero old value) and once in the real incremental shape using the branch's current remote tip as the old value, since the branch already exists remotely. Both report scan mode 'operator denylist + baseline' and exit 0: no object introduced by this range carries a denylisted term.

PUBLIC-ASSET PRIVACY -- OK, AND INDEPENDENTLY CONFIRMED. The tool reports public-privacy ok and entities-derivation ok. Because this range rewrites the law document, five skills, the behavior map and the shipped-hash manifest -- 32 public files, the largest public surface I have reviewed in this series -- I did not stop at the tool's own verdict: an independent grep across the added lines of every touched public asset for operator name, home-path prefixes, private-IP literals, sibling repo slugs, vendor and cloud hostnames and e-mail domains returns ZERO hits. A governance rewrite is precisely where a private example name tends to leak into documentation, and none did.

DEPENDENCIES -- ZERO NEW CVE SURFACE. The lock file is untouched in the range. The packaging manifest's only change is the single version line, from 0.4.5 to 0.4.6; no dependency block, extra or constraint is edited. Because no dependency moved, this range introduces no CVE surface.

THE VERSION MINT IS VERIFIED AGAINST THE LIVE INDEX, NOT THE COMMIT MESSAGE. This release mints its version at BIRTH rather than at ship, which changes when the number becomes load-bearing but not the supply-chain question, so I checked it the same way as before. The published set now ends at 0.4.5 -- the previous ship completed and is live -- the index's own latest is 0.4.5, and 0.4.6 is unclaimed. So 0.4.6 is the strict contiguous next patch: it collides with nothing, shadows nothing, and will resolve correctly as the new highest version when published. The mint-at-birth change is, if anything, safer than mint-at-ship: the number is fixed and reviewable throughout the cycle instead of appearing in the final commit.

TEST INTEGRITY -- NOTHING WAS DISABLED TO GO GREEN, AND I CHECKED THE DELETIONS INDIVIDUALLY. Zero skip, xfail or quarantine markers are added anywhere in the range. One test module was deleted (2 tests, 49 lines) and one in-file cluster was removed, and both pair with a genuine feature deletion rather than with silenced behaviour: the segment-scaffolding function they pinned no longer exists anywhere in the package (no definition survives), and the scaffolder shed 122 lines accordingly. The removed router cluster is likewise paired -- and notably its sibling test SURVIVES deliberately as a comment-honesty pin, so the deletion narrowed the cluster to what still has a subject rather than clearing it. Net coverage moves strongly positive: 2 tests removed against 15 added across three new modules, tests +270/-168 = +102 lines. The replacement modules pin exactly the new risk surface this release introduces -- the archive verb's refusals, the filename decider, and the rename rule.

BUG-SURFACE DELTA (operator standing order): REDUCED, and the headline number understates it -- evidence in metrics.bug_surface_evidence. Production is +331/-233 = net +98, but the entire increase is the NEW governance capability (the archive verb, 134 lines): excluding it, the rest of the production tree is +197/-233 = NET -36 LOC while absorbing a new filename decider and a new doctor rule. The deletions are structural, not cosmetic: the scaffolded segment lane is gone (+4/-122 in the scaffolder), the segment routing is deleted from the doctor (+50/-60), the segment field is retired from the state model, and the release-state filename gains ONE decider that every reader now goes through instead of hand-building the name. That is the same one-decider consolidation shape the previous release was praised for, applied to a new surface. No puxadinho: I found no added flag, special case, second code path or cross-feature reach-in introduced to work around a symptom -- and the one place a second path WOULD have been tempting, supporting both state-document filenames, is handled by a single read-side resolver plus a migration rule that retires the old name, rather than by a permanent branch. The open bug ledger stands at 0.

WHAT I FOUND THAT IS WRONG, HONESTLY STATED. The range deletes the segment-scaffolding function but leaves three comments that still describe it as live, one of which asserts it 'stays' and 'is exercised directly by its own unit tests' -- both clauses now false, and the second doubly so because that very test module is deleted in this same range. This is documentation drift with zero runtime or security effect, recorded LOW rather than ignored because it is exactly the defect class the range's own surviving comment-honesty test exists to prevent, and because a comment that vouches for deleted code actively misleads the next maintainer. Separately, the state-document schema still declares the retired segment property; I examined whether that is drift and concluded the property's PRESENCE is correct and deliberate -- the schema forbids additional properties, so removing it would make every pre-0.4.6 document fail validation, and it is absent from the required list so new documents may omit it -- while only its description text, which still presents the field as active, is stale. Both are recorded below for the operator to dispose of; neither is ship-blocking and neither is a security defect.

GENERATED-FILE LEAKAGE -- NONE. The range commits nothing under the runtime state directory, and no virtualenv, bytecode, cache, log, coverage or test-results artifact appears in it.

CHAIN OF CUSTODY. This verdict names 90146c64, the current branch head, and is written to the LIVE release's verdict directory because 0.4.6 is not archived. If the PR head advances, a new verdict naming the new head (or one whose first parent is the named sha) is required. Like any verdict it is consumed once by the merge and must be deleted immediately after -- a survivor becomes a standing authorization credential, the CWE-613 condition this project closed two releases ago.

findings.detail_md:
CWE-1116 (inaccurate comments) -- documentation drift, **no runtime or security consequence**.

**Verified, not inferred.** A package-wide search finds no `def scaffold_release_segment` anywhere; only three comment references survive:

| Location | What it still claims |
|---|---|
| `dadaia_workspace/cli/commands/specs.py` (~line 27) | that the function `stays -- it still scaffolds the SPEC/PLAN/TASKS stubs of a dir-based segment ... and is exercised directly by its own unit tests` |
| `dadaia_workspace/features/specs/canon.py` (~line 345) | references it as the mechanism that opens a segment |
| `dadaia_workspace/features/specs/doctor_common.py` (~line 129) | references it as a live scaffolder entry point |

The first is the misleading one: **both** of its clauses are now false, and the second is false *because of this range* -- the module that exercised it (`tests/unit/features/specs/test_scaffold_segment.py`) is deleted here.

A related smaller instance: `tests/unit/features/specs/test_doctor.py` retains a section header for a segmented-release pair whose body was removed.

**Why this is recorded rather than waved through.** This is precisely the defect class the range's own surviving test `test_stale_check_9_comment_no_longer_claims_coverage_it_does_not_provide` exists to prevent -- a comment vouching for coverage or code that is not there. The range fixed one instance of that class while leaving three more of it. A comment that vouches for deleted code is a trap for the next maintainer and a small but real contributor to bug surface.

**Not blocking:** no mandatory REQUEST_CHANGES trigger applies -- no secret, no gate failure, no privacy issue, no disabled test, no untrusted-input sink.
findings.fix_recommendation: Delete or correct the three stale references (and the orphaned section header) so no comment vouches for the removed function -- ideally in this candidate, since the deletion that invalidated them ships here. If the surviving comment-honesty pin can be generalised cheaply to assert that no comment names a symbol absent from the package, that would convert this recurring class from review-caught to mechanically caught; propose it rather than bolt it on if it would grow the test's scope.

findings.message: Positive, and the decisive security check for this range: the new file-moving verb is confined to its release directory BY CONSTRUCTION -- every path component is a directory-entry name, an integer, or a module constant. Traversal is structurally impossible, not merely validated against.
findings.detail_md:
CWE-22 (path traversal) and CWE-59 (symlink following) -- **both structurally excluded**, reported as the positive result of the review's highest-risk item.

A verb that renames documents into a computed directory is where a traversal defect would live, so every component of the destination path was traced to its origin:

| Component | Origin | Can it contain a separator or `..`? |
|---|---|---|
| specs directory | caller, from context resolution (workspace-local) | n/a -- the confinement root |
| release identifier | a directory-entry NAME from iterating the releases directory | **No** -- an iteration entry is always a single component, never `.` or `..` |
| candidate folder | `f"rc-{rc}"` where `rc` is an **int** = 1 + max of ints parsed by an anchored `^rc-(\d+)$` | **No** -- an integer cannot introduce a separator |
| document names | module-level constants | **No** |

There is no concatenation of caller-supplied text anywhere in the path, so the destination is provably `<specs>/releases/<one component>/rc-<int>/<constant>`. This is stronger than a validation check, which can be bypassed or drift out of agreement with its caller.

**Three further safety properties, present and deliberate:**

1. The candidate directory is created with a bare make-directory call -- **no** parent creation and **no** exist-tolerance -- so it refuses loudly rather than clobbering an existing directory or materialising a path elsewhere.
2. The rename primitive used for the move **does not follow a symlink at the source**; it relocates the link itself. A planted symlink in the trio would therefore be moved, never written through to an external target.
3. Removal of the superseded legacy document uses an unlink, which likewise removes the link rather than the target.

**The validation gate in front of the move is real and tested:** the verb refuses unless exactly one live release exists, the trio is present, no task marker is open or reserved, and the phase is closure; an ambiguous multiple-live-release tree is reported as an explicit error rather than guessed at. Four of the seven new tests for the module exercise refusal paths.
findings.fix_recommendation: No action. Recorded as the measured basis for clearing the range's highest-risk change.

findings.message: Positive: the new doctor auto-fix renames using a final-component replacement, so the rename cannot be aimed outside the source file's own directory regardless of the path the issue carries.
findings.detail_md:
CWE-22 -- **structurally excluded** for the second file-mutating path in the range.

The fix resolves the issue's path, re-checks that it is a regular file, and renames it to a sibling using an operation that **substitutes only the final path component and preserves the parent directory**. The destination is therefore always in the source's own directory; there is no way to redirect it elsewhere even with a hostile issue path.

Confinement is doubled rather than singular: the issue's path is not external input either -- the check that emits it derives it as `<specs>/releases/<release identifier>/<legacy constant>`, where the release identifier comes from the same directory-entry-name derivation described above.

Two local-only theoretical notes, recorded for completeness rather than as defects, because both require write access to the operator's own release directory -- at which point an actor can write anywhere directly, so the trust boundary is unchanged:

- The check emits the issue only when the canonical filename is absent, and the fix runs later in the same process; a same-directory replacement between those two moments is a narrow time-of-check-to-time-of-use window.
- The canonical document is written with an ordinary text write, which *does* follow a symlink at the destination; a symlink planted at that exact name would be written through. The project already has an explicit symlink doctrine in its handoff-deletion lane, so the pattern is understood here -- this is a defense-in-depth note, not a live exposure.
findings.fix_recommendation: No action required. If the operator ever wants the write path to match the deletion lane's existing symlink doctrine, the cheap hardening is to refuse when the canonical target exists and is a symlink -- a single guard, not a second code path.

findings.detail_md:
Supply-chain integrity **confirmation**, checked against the live index rather than the commit message, consistent with prior cycles.

| Question | Measured answer |
|---|---|
| Index latest | `0.4.5` |
| Is `0.4.5` published? | **Yes** -- the previous ship completed |
| Is `0.4.6` taken? | **No** |
| Relationship | strict contiguous next patch |

So `0.4.6` collides with nothing, shadows nothing, and will resolve as the new highest version when published. There is no repeat of the shadowing risk considered in the previous cycle, because the number moves forward rather than backward.

**On the mint-at-birth change.** This release deletes mint-at-ship and fixes the version when the release is born. From a supply-chain standpoint this is neutral-to-positive: the number that will be published is present and reviewable throughout the whole cycle, and appears in every review of the release, instead of materialising in a final commit that historically received the least scrutiny. The dependency surface is unaffected -- the manifest's only change in the range is that one line, and the lock file is untouched.
findings.fix_recommendation: No action. Recorded as the measured basis for the version carried by this candidate.

findings.message: Examined and cleared: the state-document schema still declares the retired segment property. Its PRESENCE is correct and load-bearing for backward compatibility; only its description text is stale.
findings.detail_md:
Investigated as suspected drift, and it is **mostly not** drift -- recorded with the reasoning so it is not mistakenly 'cleaned up' into a breaking change.

The schema forbids additional properties and lists the required keys explicitly. Given that:

- `segment` is **absent from the required list**, so a new document that omits it validates cleanly -- which is what the retirement needs.
- `segment` is **present in the declared properties**, and because additional properties are forbidden, **removing it would make every pre-0.4.6 document that still carries the field fail validation outright**. Keeping it declared is what allows a legacy document to keep validating, matching the state module's own stated posture that a legacy document still parses and the key is simply ignored.

So the property should stay. What *is* stale is its description, which still presents the field as an active feature ('the active dir-based segment ... when the release's SPEC/PLAN/TASKS live under a segment directory') rather than as a retired field retained for compatibility. That is the same documentation-honesty class as the LOW above, at lower stakes.
findings.fix_recommendation: Do NOT remove the property -- that would break validation of existing documents under the forbid-additional-properties rule. Reword its description to state that the field is retired as of 0.4.6, ignored by readers, and retained only so legacy documents continue to validate.

Both hold, so `fe04319a..384dc391` is the complete content surface and nothing was hidden inside the reconciliation merge -- the failure mode this check exists to catch. Reviewing the head against the integration branch would have surfaced the same content plus reconciliation noise; the range actually reviewed is both correct and tighter.

Also confirmed: the four archived state-document renames are pure renames (100% similarity, zero content change), so no archived release's recorded state was altered while its filename was migrated.
